1.pericope_label: Boaz the kinsman is introduced, and Ruth asks leave to glean, lighting by chance on his field

schools.summary: Henry notes that the Chaldee renders the phrase mighty in the law, and that if Boaz was both it was a most rare and excellent conjunction, to be mighty in wealth and mighty in the scriptures too, for those that are so are mighty indeed; the man carries might in his very name. He presses the silence of the town: the Bethlehemites would have done well to invite Naomi and her daughter-in-law first to one good house and then to another, which would have supported an aged widow and encouraged a new convert, but instead of tasting the dainties of Canaan they had no way of getting necessary food but by gleaning, and for all that appears they might have starved — God has chosen the poor of this world, and poor they are likely to be, for though God has chosen them men commonly overlook them. He draws two warnings from the kinship, that the great should not be ashamed to own kindred who are mean and despised, lest they be found proud and unnatural, and that the poor who have rich relations should neither be proud of the connection nor trust to it, since it is the wise providence of God that makes the difference. On Ruth herself he dwells on her humility: she did not say that to glean, which is in effect to beg, she was ashamed, nor tell her mother she had never been brought up to live upon crumbs, but cheerfully stooped to the meanness of her circumstances, and it was her own motion and not her mother’s injunction — high spirits can more easily starve than stoop, and before Ruth’s honour was this humility. He adds that she was not mindful of the country from which she came out, though she now had a fair occasion to return to it.

Ellicott supplies the pedigree and its difficulty: by the line given at the close of the book Boaz is grandson of the Nahshon who was prince of the tribe of Judah during the wanderings, and son of Salmon and Rahab of Jericho, which crowds the generations — a difficulty he thinks eased by supposing the last two to be children of their fathers’ old age, any gaps in the genealogy belonging rather to its earlier portion. On Ruth’s request he finds her character coming out strongly, since she does not hesitate to face the hard work necessary on her mother-in-law’s account, nor is she too proud to condescend to work which might seem humiliating, nor does she hanker after her old home in Moab and the plenty there: energy, honesty of purpose and loyalty are alike evinced. On the chance that brought her to the field he will not leave the two words side by side: her hap happened, he grants, a chance in outward seeming, yet a clear shaping of her course by unseen hands, her steps divinely guided to a certain field that God’s purposes should be worked out. Keil and Delitzsch explain that the statement about the kinsman was necessary to make the whole occurrence intelligible, and set out the legal position of gleaning: the Mosaic law expressly secured the poor their right to glean and forbade the owners to glean their own fields, but hard-hearted farmers and reapers threw obstacles in the way of the poor and even forbade them altogether, which is why Ruth proposed to glean after whoever should generously allow it. Of her arrival they give the Hebrew bluntly, that her chance chanced to hit upon the field, she knowing neither the owner nor his connection with Elimelech.

Gill finds the situation strange on both sides. Naomi made no application to a kinsman who was well known to her, which might arise from her modesty and a reluctance to be troublesome to a relation of her husband’s rather than of her own family; and what is stranger, this kinsman took no notice of her and sent nothing, generous and liberal though he was, and though he had heard the character of Ruth — unless, Gill suggests, he was simply not acquainted with their indigent circumstances. Of Ruth he says she was unwilling to live an idle life and ready to do anything for the support of herself and her ancient mother-in-law, which was very commendable and showed her an industrious virtuous woman; and he guards the mention of her many children in the complaint of others, since a numerous offspring was always reckoned a blessing among the Jews. He reports from the Midrash the homelier detail that she marked the ways as she went before entering the field, and came back to observe the marks and signs.

Clarke confirms the fragility of a gleaner’s right from nearer home: the practice was long a general custom in England and Ireland, supposed to be a right recognised by law, but it is now settled by a solemn judgment of the court of common pleas that no right to glean can be claimed at common law, any man being free to permit or prevent it in his own ground, while Irish statutes have restricted it so far as to prohibit it; and Ruth’s phrasing, he adds, seems to intimate that notwithstanding the law of Moses the gleaners might be prevented by the owner. He reports the opinion that Boaz was one of the judges of Israel and allows at least that he was a man of considerable property, and of her arrival he sets the two words side by side, that she was accidentally or providentially led to that part of the country which belonged to Boaz. Wesley reads her request as modesty rather than doubt, that though it was their duty to permit this she thought it might perhaps be denied her, and that it became her humbly to acknowledge their kindness; she was not ashamed to confess her poverty, nor would she eat the bread of idleness. On the chance he makes a rule of the distinction: it was a chance in reference to second causes but ordered by God’s providence, since God wisely orders small events, even those that seem altogether contingent, and many a great affair is brought about by a little turn, fortuitous as to men but designed by God.

debates.question: Why had neither Naomi nor Boaz approached the other?

positions.view: Her modesty and reluctance to trouble a relation of her husband’s; and he perhaps did not know their indigent circumstances
The fault lay with the town, which should have taken them in; God has chosen the poor, yet men commonly overlook them
Secured by the Mosaic law, but obstructed and even forbidden in practice by hard-hearted farmers and reapers
No such right exists at common law; any owner may permit or prevent it, and Ruth’s wording implies the same of Israel
Permitted to the poor and the stranger, though she thought it might still be denied her

Alone in testing the gleaner’s right against English and Irish law, where a judgment of the common pleas had lately denied it.
Alone in reporting the Midrash that she marked the ways as she went, and alone in finding Boaz’s own silence strange.

4.pericope_label: Boaz greets his reapers, asks after Ruth, blesses her and bids her eat with his people

schools.summary: Clarke calls the salutation worthy of particular regard, gives both halves in the Hebrew, and asks whether a pious mind can read such godly salutations without wishing for a return of those simple primitive times, paraphrasing the one as a prayer for preservation and strength in the work and the other for increase of the field and grace to use the bounty to the glory of the giver. He takes the man set over the reapers for a kind of steward or hind with the under management of the estate, and finds the whole scene figured on the shield of Achilles, where the man in charge is called king and his staff a sceptre and stands in mute dignity merely to see the work well done, and where, he thinks, there are gleaners too in the boys who gather the handfuls after the binders. On the blessing he takes the sheltering wings from the young of fowls, which on sighting a bird of prey run to their mother to be covered, and shelter so from storms as well, and infers that Ruth had already attached herself to the Jewish religion. He explains her prostration as the custom of the East when inferiors approached those of superior rank, and reports the Targum’s expansion of the exchange, where Ruth asks how she has found grace, being a daughter of Moab, of whom it is said that the unclean shall not enter the congregation of the Lord, and Boaz answers that what the Lord decreed he decreed of the men and not the women, and that it had been told him by prophecy that kings and prophets should proceed from her. Of the meal he takes the chomez for a refreshing acid sauce in which the reapers dipped their bread, cooling them as they ate. Wesley notes that master and men expressed their piety even in their civil conversation and worldly transactions, which now so many are ashamed of; that Ruth did not boldly intrude herself but modestly asked leave; that she was not retired through idleness, having been diligent and constant in her labours, the house being the little house or tent set up in the fields at such times and necessary in those hot countries, where labourers might retire for a little repose or repast. On the wings he allows Clarke’s figure but sets another beside it, the wings of the Cherubim between which God dwelt; and he reads her answer as a humble imploring of the continuance of a good opinion she thinks undeserved, being a person more mean and obscure, a stranger born of heathen parents.

Henry finds a great deal of decency in Boaz’s carriage both towards his own servants and towards this poor stranger. Of the servants he observes that harvest-time is a busy time and that in great families it is requisite there should be one to oversee the rest and appoint to each their portion both of work and meat, ministers being such servants in God’s house; and that Boaz came himself to his reapers, which was both his own interest, since he that wholly leaves his business to others will have it done by the halves and the master’s eye makes a fat horse, and also for their encouragement, since masters who live at ease should think with tenderness of those that toil for them and bear the burden and heat of the day. In the exchange of blessings he reads a whole household in good order: Boaz did not fall a chiding them as if he came only to find fault but prayed for them, and they did not, as soon as he was out of hearing, fall a cursing him, as some ill-natured servants do that hate their master’s eye, but returned his courtesy — things are likely to go well in a house where there is such good-will between master and servants, and they showed not only their courtesy but their piety, acknowledging that all good comes from the presence and blessing of God. But Henry alone adds a caution: such pious ejaculations must not degenerate into formality, lest in them we take the name of the Lord our God in vain, though if we are serious in them we may keep up our communion with God and fetch in mercy and grace from him.

Ellicott finds in the greeting a trace of the good feeling prevailing between Boaz and his servants: though he has come to supervise the work it is not in a fault-finding spirit but with true courtesy and friendliness, nor in a frivolous jesting manner, but with gravity and soberness he presents a true gentleman in his intercourse with his inferiors. On the blessing he keeps to the logic of the prayer, that Boaz asks a recompense for her dutifulness the more readily because she has herself put herself under God’s protection, faith in divine help and grace being sure of an undoubted recompense. He notes that her foreignness was less of a barrier than it sounds, since the Moabite tongue, for all its peculiarities, differed but little from Hebrew, as may be seen from the famous inscription of King Mesha discovered in the land of Moab; and that the word rendered friendly is literally unto the heart, the same phrase being rendered comfortably by the prophet. Keil and Delitzsch hear the patriarch behind the blessing: in leaving father and mother and the land of her nativity for a people she knew not heretofore, Ruth had done what God commanded Abraham to do, the full reward Boaz wishes her recalls the promise made to Abraham, and the sheltering wings come from the song of Moses — words in which, they say, we see the genuine piety of a true Israelite. They catch how she takes her own words back, since having called herself his maiden she adds that she is not like one of his maidens, restricting the expression, as an older commentator saw: what am I saying when I call myself thy maiden, being unworthy to be compared with the least of them. Of the meal they make the chomez a sour beverage of vinegar or sour wine mixed with oil, a very refreshing drink still a favourite in the East, and the parched corn roasted grains of wheat still eaten by reapers on the harvest field.

Gill has Boaz come into the field to see how his workmen went on and to encourage them by his presence and courteous behaviour, and to see what provisions were wanting, it being near noon; and though a man of great wealth he did not think it below him to look after his servants, which showed his diligence and industry as well as his humility. He gathers the same proverb from the ancients: a king in Homer is represented among his reapers with his sceptre in his hand and cheerful, Pliny reports it as a saying of old that the eye of the master is the most fruitful thing in the field, and Aristotle tells of a Persian asked what most fattened a horse who answered, the eye of the master, and an African asked the best dung for land who answered, the steps of his master. Of the overseer he notes that Josephus calls him the man who had the care of the field and all things relating to it, and that the Jews say he was set over forty-two persons; and that this servant had taken a great deal of notice of Ruth and conversed with her, and so was capable of answering his master’s question.

positions.view: As a godly salutation to be wished back: can a pious mind read it without longing for those simple primitive times?
As evidence of a household in good order, but with the caution that such ejaculations must not degenerate into formality
As piety carried into civil conversation, which now so many are ashamed of
As the mark of a true gentleman with his inferiors, neither fault-finding nor frivolous

17.pericope_label: Ruth beats out her ephah and brings it home, Naomi learns whose field it was and names Boaz a near kinsman

schools.summary: Henry notices how little she took of what was offered: though Boaz had ordered his servants to leave handfuls for her she went on gleaning the scattered ears, and scarcely used, much less abused, his kindness. She gleaned until evening, making no excuse to sit still or go home early, for we must not be weary of well-doing; she threshed the corn herself so as to carry it the more easily and have it ready for use, since the slothful man roasts not that which he took in hunting and so loses the benefit of it, while the substance of a diligent man is precious; and she carried it into the city herself, though had she asked it some of Boaz’s servants would likely have done it for her — we should study to be as little troublesome as possible to those who are kind to us. Many a little, he adds, makes a great deal, and in all labour, even that of gleaning, there is profit. Of the homecoming he marks that she went straight home and did not stay to converse with Boaz’s servants, and that she showed her mother-in-law what she had gleaned so that Naomi might see she had not been idle; and that she entertained her with what she had left of the good dinner, so that having shown industry abroad she showed piety at home, which is part of the honour children owe their parents. The gleanings a righteous man has, he observes, are better than the harvests of many wicked.

Ellicott explains that she threshed the barley herself so as to save the labour of carrying away the straw, and reckons the ephah at rather more than four pecks. He raises a difficulty at the blessing which the others pass over: it is not clear whether the grammatical antecedent of the one who has not left off his kindness to the living and the dead is God or Boaz, though either way a good sense is obtained — as our lost dear ones had kindness shown them of old, so we too now. If Boaz is the antecedent, he finds it curious that Naomi, knowing she dwelt near a kinsman of her husband’s who had shown kindness before they departed to Moab, should not have made herself known to him, which is at any rate a proof of the independence of her character; and he observes that the name once named evidently suggests the train of thought which at length leads Naomi to appeal to him for a kinsman’s special aid, the aid of the redeemer. He renders the phrase one of our next kinsmen as one of those who must redeem. On Naomi’s advice he notes that she speaks of the young women where Ruth had spoken of the young men, and that no distinction need be intended, Ruth naming the men as the chief workers and Naomi the women as those with whom Ruth would be specially thrown; and that to glean in another field would not only be throwing away genuine kindness but contemptuously proclaiming the fact. Keil and Delitzsch fasten on the odd verb, that she drew out — from her pocket, as the Chaldee rightly supplies — what she had left over from her sufficiency, meaning the parched corn Boaz had reached her at the meal. They have Naomi reason from the evidence, conjecturing from the quantity of barley collected and the food brought home that someone had taken notice of Ruth, and then, on hearing the name, seeing that this relative of her husband had been chosen by God to be a benefactor of them both. They explain her satisfaction with the arrangement, since Ruth would thereby be secured from the insults she might receive gleaning in strange fields, the verb meaning to fall upon and ill-treat; and they hear in the closing remark that she dwelt with her mother-in-law a tacit allusion to the change that came for Ruth once the harvest was over.

Clarke puts the ephah at not less than seven gallons and a half and calls it a good day’s work; he explains that as Ruth had received a distinct portion at dinner-time, of which she had more than she could eat, she brought the rest home to her mother-in-law. He identifies the parties in the blessing plainly, that Naomi and Ruth were the living and also the representatives of Elimelech and Mahlon, who were dead, Naomi being of the family and Ruth, though not of it, the widow of one of its deceased branches. The word kinsman he unpacks at length as one of our redeemers, a near kinsman who by the Mosaic law had the right to redeem a forfeited inheritance, and he sets out the threefold office: to buy back the forfeited inheritance or the liberty of one who had been obliged to sell himself for a servant, to avenge the blood of a murdered relative by killing the slayer if he found him outside the cities of refuge, and to take the widow of a brother or relative who died childless, the children of that marriage being reputed the deceased brother’s; and he notes that a nearest kinsman who refused was treated with indignity, lost his right to the inheritance, and left the way open to the next after him, which is how the case of Boaz comes about. Wesley reads the reserved portion as what was left at dinner after she had eaten and was sufficed, and turns Naomi’s question into a nightly examination: it is a good question to ask ourselves in the evening, where have I gleaned to-day, what improvements have I made in grace or knowledge, what have I learned or done which will turn to account? Of the kindness to the dead he reads one continued thing, shown formerly to the husband and his sons while they lived and not withdrawn now; and of the advice to stay in Boaz’s field, that to go elsewhere would expose her to inconveniences from strangers and incur his displeasure, as if she despised his kindness.

Gill has Naomi observe the charge Boaz had given and think fit to advise her daughter-in-law upon it, and sums Ruth’s conduct through the whole as accepting the kindness of Boaz, attending to the advice of her mother-in-law, and using all diligence to get a livelihood for them both, in which she was a wonderful instance of dutiful affection, humility and industry.

outliers.claim: Alone in finding the antecedent of the blessing ambiguous, and alone in reading Naomi’s long silence toward her kinsman as a proof of the independence of her character.
Alone in setting out the threefold office of the redeemer at length, including the avenger’s right outside the cities of refuge.
Alone in turning Naomi’s question into a nightly self-examination: where have I gleaned to-day?
